```{r setup}
library(tines)
```

A **schema** records a data analysis as an ordered sequence of decisions,
each written in natural language. It is the central object in `tines`: code
is generated from it, and it is what an alternatives file modifies to
produce a multiverse. This vignette covers

  * the anatomy of a schema YAML file,
  * the five ways to create one -- from a template, in R, from a file, from
    a data frame, or from prose with an LLM,
  * how a schema can optionally be mapped to a dataset, and
  * how pairing one with an alternatives file turns it into a multiverse.

# The big picture

A schema file has two parts: a `meta` block marking the document as a
schema, and a `nodes` list holding the steps of the analysis. The skeleton
always looks like this:

```yaml
meta:
  type: schema
  name: <optional label for the analysis>
nodes:
  - id: <step id>
    objective: <the problem this step solves>
    decision: <what was done>
    rationale: <why it was done that way>
  - id: <step id>
    ...
```

Each step carries four fields:

* **`id`** names the step. Ids must be unique within a schema, and they are
  how an alternatives file points at the step it overrides.
* **`objective`** states the problem the step addresses -- the question, not
  the answer.
* **`decision`** records what was actually done.
* **`rationale`** records why it was done that way. This is the field that
  lets a reader agree or disagree with a choice, rather than only observe it.

You can initialize the template above via `draft_tines()`, and 
fill in the steps by hand. Apart from that, there are four ways to create a schema: 


| If you are starting from | Use |
|----|----|
| nothing, and you would rather write YAML | `draft_tines()`, fill in the template, then `read_tines()` |
| nothing, and you would rather work in R | `build_schema()`, then one `add_step()` per decision |
| a schema file written earlier | `read_tines(path)` |
| a table of decisions, say from a spreadsheet | `as_schema(df)` |
| prose, such as a manuscript's methods section | `extract_schema(text, data_dict)` |

All five converge on the same thing: a `schema` object, which is a tibble
of steps. The YAML file is the format you store and share; the object is
what you work with in R. Most functions that consume a schema (`expand_tines()`, `gen_code()`,
`draw_tines()`) take either. Below we show examples of creating a schema in each of the five ways.

# Creating a schema

## From a template

`draft_tines()` writes a skeleton with two placeholder steps, ready to fill
in by hand:

```{r}
draft_path <- withr::local_tempfile(fileext = ".yml")
draft_tines(file_path = draft_path)
```

```{r results = "asis", echo = FALSE}
cat("```yaml\n")
cat(readLines(draft_path), sep = "\n")
cat("\n```\n")
```

## In R

`build_schema()` starts an empty schema and `add_step()` appends to it, one
step per decision:

```{r}
hdi <- build_schema(name = "HDI Example") |>
  add_step(
    id = "step-scaling",
    objective = "variables are in different scales",
    decision = "apply min-max scaling to each variable",
    rationale = "to put them on the same scale for combination"
  ) |>
  add_step(
    id = "step-combine",
    objective = "combine the three dimensions into a single index",
    decision = "use the geometric mean",
    rationale = "the geometric mean penalizes uneven development"
  )
hdi
```

`write_tines()` writes it back out as YAML:

```{r}
out_path <- withr::local_tempfile(fileext = ".yml")
write_tines(hdi, out_path)
```

```{r results = "asis", echo = FALSE}
cat("```yaml\n")
cat(readLines(out_path), sep = "\n")
cat("\n```\n")
```

## From a file

Most often the schema already exists. `read_tines()` reads one in -- here
the Human Development Index example shipped with the package, which
combines health, education, and standard of living into a single index:

```{r results = "asis", echo = FALSE}
schema_path <- system.file("hdi.yml", package = "tines")
cat("```yaml\n")
cat(readLines(schema_path), sep = "\n")
cat("\n```\n")
```

```{r}
schema <- read_tines(schema_path)
schema
```

Because the result is a tibble, the decisions of an analysis can be
inspected with the tools you already use for data frames:

```{r}
schema$id
schema$rationale[schema$id == "step-combine"]
```


## From a data frame

Decisions are often catalogued somewhere else first -- a spreadsheet, or a
table in a lab notebook. Any data frame carrying the four step fields
coerces directly:

```{r}
steps <- data.frame(
  id = c("step-clean", "step-model"),
  objective = c("handle missing values", "estimate the effect"),
  decision = c("drop incomplete cases", "fit a linear model"),
  rationale = c("listwise deletion keeps the sample interpretable",
                "the relationship is assumed linear")
)

as_schema(steps, name = "From a spreadsheet")
```

`inputs` and `outputs` may be supplied as list-columns if you have them;
otherwise add them later with `update_io()`. A data frame missing any of
the four required fields is refused, and says which:

```{r error = TRUE}
as_schema(steps[, c("id", "decision")])
```

## From a manuscript, with an LLM

`extract_schema()` drafts a schema from a prose description of the
methodology, such as the methods section of a paper:

```{r eval = FALSE}
# Requires an LLM API key (e.g. ANTHROPIC_API_KEY); not run automatically.
extract_schema(
  text = football_grp5,
  data_dict = c("player", "redCards", "rater1", "rater2"),
  output_file = tempfile(fileext = ".yml")
)
```

A schema drafted this way carries extra bookkeeping fields -- `confidence`
and `clarification_question` -- recording how sure the model was that it read
each decision correctly. Any extra field is preserved as
its own column when the file is read, and written back out unchanged:

```{r}
drafted <- example_football_grp5()
colnames(drafted)
```

# Mapping a schema to data

A schema's four core fields describe an analysis without reference to any
dataset, and that is enough to generate code: `gen_code()` leaves the LLM to
work out which variables each step uses, and `validate_script()` then runs
the script on the real data. Optionally, a schema can also record the data
it runs on and be *mapped*, giving every step the variables it reads
(`inputs`) and creates (`outputs`):

```yaml
meta:
  type: schema
  name: HDI
  data:
    source: data/hdi.csv
nodes:
- id: step-scaling
  objective: variables are in different scales
  decision: apply min-max scaling to each variable
  rationale: to put them on the same scale for combination
  inputs: [life_exp, exp_sch, gni]
  outputs: [scaled]
```

A mapped schema can be checked against its data before any code is
generated, and `draw_tines()` draws it by data flow rather than by step
order. Most schemas are never mapped. If you write a schema by hand, we
recommend leaving inputs and outputs out, since they are easy to get wrong.
If an LLM drafts it and is given the data, it maps the variables as well.
Either way, you can review the inputs and outputs and modify them.

The data a schema runs on is a data file (`.csv`, `.rds`, `.rda`), a package
dataset (`"VGAMdata::smqP"`), an R script that creates the data, or a data
frame. The schema keeps only this reference and the data's column names,
never the data itself. A file path is written relative to the YAML file, so
the two can be moved together; a data frame has no reference that can be
written down. `gen_code()` uses the reference to load the data, so it is
worth setting even on a schema that is not mapped.

# From one schema to many

A schema describes one analysis. Pairing it with an **alternatives file** --
which records different ways of carrying out one or more of its steps --
and passing both to `expand_tines()` produces a `multiverse`, one schema per
branch the alternatives file describes, alongside the original:

```{r}
alts <- read_alternatives(system.file("hdi-alt-single.yml", package = "tines"))
expand_tines(schema, alts)
```

See `vignette("alternatives")` for the anatomy of an alternatives file and
the two ways it can be expanded.
